chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
title: Working with piano players; no strap; Meade Lux Lewis
summary: Rosenberg says Bunn's single-string style suits pianists; Bunn knew where the four beats were, and held the guitar with his elbow and no strap.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: This has got is good. Meade Lux Lewis on this one.
Yeah.
You worked with a lot of different piano players.
What?
You worked with a lot of different piano players.
Yeah.
In some ways I think that you were one of the most successful guitarists in this style, working with a piano player, because you don't play that many chords.
Yeah.
So you don't get in each other's way. You're playing the single string, you know.
Yeah. When you took a solo, I'm ready to take a solo.
All the fills kind of get you warmed up.
Yeah.
Outlines the tune.
That's right. The best thing, I can hear it. Good thing I know where four beats is.
What's that?
I know where four beats is. How the hell I know that, I don't know. It had to be a gift. I had to stay close to that. You can tell by the way I'm bearing down on it.
Yeah. The snapping sound some time.
Yeah.
Did you have a strap or did you just hold it up without a strap?
Without a strap.
With your elbow.
With my elbow.
Right. That's hard, because of the way you use your fingers, you know?
Yeah.
It must have been uncomfortable sometimes.
It was. That's why you'd see me loaded all the time. Hear the way he said that? (Singing) -- "I'm confessing that I love you. Da, da, da, da, de, de, de."
"Basin Street."
"Basin Street."
